lead: Auto Layout turns every view's position and size into linear equations called constraints. Instead of a fixed frame, you state rules — this button sits 16 points from the leading edge, that label is centred — and the system solves them for whatever screen it meets. The same rules survive rotation, a bigger phone, or split screen. Stack views bundle the common cases into one object with an axis, alignment and distribution. Every iOS screen relies on this, from a UPI confirmation to an IRCTC train list.
prereq: You need Chapter 6.5 for views and view controllers, and Chapter 6.6 for the controls being constrained.

blocks.text: Most constraints are linear equations over a view's frame; a constraint may also be an inequality such as height ≥ 44, which the solver satisfies rather than solves exactly. The attributes are leading, trailing, top, bottom, width, height, centerX and centerY. Leading is the side writing starts from — left in English, right in Arabic — so leading-based layouts mirror themselves.

blocks.where: item1 and item2 are views, usually a child and its superview; attr is one of the eight attributes; m is the multiplier (default 1); c is the constant in points. Pinning a button 16 points in from the leading edge is button.leading = safeArea.leading + 16.

blocks.text: The safe area is the part of the screen not covered by the notch, status bar or home indicator. Pin to view.safeAreaLayoutGuide, not to view, or the top row slides under the sensor housing.

A label or button also carries an intrinsic content size — the size its text and font ask for. Two priorities arbitrate when space is short. Content hugging (default 250) resists growing; a higher value keeps the view small. Compression resistance (default 750) resists shrinking; a higher value refuses to squash. Priority 1000 is UILayoutPriority.required — the strongest wish, and you cannot soften it by lowering it. If required rules conflict, the system still breaks one at runtime and logs the conflict, so the fix is to remove or rewrite it.

An ambiguous layout has more than one solution and shows as orange or dashed lines. Fix it by adding a rule — pin both leading and trailing, or give an explicit width or height — because the system needs one more equation to reach a single solution. An unsatisfiable layout has contradictory rules; fix it by deleting or lowering the priority of a conflicting rule. The runtime also breaks one and logs it.
A UIStackView arranges its arrangedSubviews in a row or column and writes the constraints itself.

items: alignment — placement on the other axis: .fill stretches children across it; also .center, .leading, .trailing.

distribution — .fill (the arranged subviews stretch to fill the axis; the child with the lowest content hugging priority, default 250, takes the slack, and the one with the lowest compression resistance shrinks when space is short), .fillEqually (every child equal), .equalSpacing (children keep intrinsic size, gaps equalise).
spacing — a constant number of points between neighbours.

blocks.text: Nest a horizontal stack inside a vertical stack to build a form without a dozen hand-written constraints. Setting isHidden = true on an arranged subview removes it from the layout; alpha = 0 does not.

A fixed frame such as CGRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: 100, height: 40) is in points and never updates. After rotation, or on a 320-point phone instead of a 430-point one, it is simply wrong. Constraints re-solve on every size change.

blocks.where: W is the container width in points, L and R the leading and trailing margins, s the spacing, n the number of arranged subviews, and w the width of each.

blocks.text: With n = 3, s = 8, L = R = 16 on W = 360: 360 − 32 = 328 content, minus 16 of gaps = 312, so w = 104 points.

figure.caption: Margins and gaps come off first: on 360 points, 360 − 32 − 16 = 312, so each button is 104 points; the same rules on 320 points give 272 ÷ 3 ≈ 90.67 points.

spec.aria: Two screen bars drawn to scale, 360 and 320 points wide, each with 16 point margins, two 8 point gaps and three equal buttons of 104 and 90.67 points.

examples.question: A horizontal stack view holds three buttons, spacing 8 points, pinned 16 points from the leading and trailing safe-area edges, distribution fillEqually. Find each button's width on a 360-point-wide screen and on a 320-point-wide screen.
steps: On 360 points: 360 − 16 − 16 = 328 points of content width.
examples.answer: Each button is 104 points on a 360-point screen and about 90.67 points on a 320-point screen.
examples.check:
W1, W2 = 360, 320
L = R = 16
s, n = 8, 3
gaps = s * (n - 1)
w1 = (W1 - L - R - gaps) / n
w2 = (W2 - L - R - gaps) / n
print(w1)
print(round(w2, 2))

traps: Pinning to view instead of view.safeAreaLayoutGuide: on a notched iPhone the top row slides under the sensor housing.
Giving a label both a fixed width and a trailing pin: the layout turns unsatisfiable. Delete one rule; do not shrink the font.
Swapping priorities: hugging 250 resists growing, compression resistance 750 resists shrinking.
Expecting .equalSpacing to equalise widths; it equalises gaps.
Dividing the full screen width by n and forgetting margins and gaps.

quiz.a: The size a view prefers from its own content, such as a label's text and font, before external constraints act.

quiz.q: State the default content hugging and compression resistance priorities.
Why pin to leading rather than left?
quiz.a: Leading follows the writing direction, so the layout mirrors correctly in right-to-left languages. Left stays physically left.

quiz.q: A 375-point screen, three buttons, spacing 10, margins 20 each side, fillEqually. Width of each?
quiz.a: 375 − 40 = 335 points of content. Two gaps = 20. 335 − 20 = 315. 315 ÷ 3 = 105 points each.

quiz.q: A label has leading = 16 and trailing = −16 to its superview, plus a fixed width of 100, on a 320-point screen. What happens?
quiz.a: The pins demand 320 − 32 = 288 points, the fixed width demands 100; the rules contradict. The layout is unsatisfiable, the runtime breaks one constraint and logs it. Delete the width.

quiz.q: Why does a frame set in viewDidLoad look wrong after rotation?
quiz.a: The frame is written once in points. Rotation changes the bounds and nothing recomputes it. Constraints re-solve; frames do not.

quiz.q: What does isHidden = true do to an arranged subview?
quiz.a: It removes the view from the layout and the stack redistributes the freed space. Setting alpha = 0 would leave the space empty.

beyond: Not for the exam. Auto Layout's solver is the Cassowary linear-constraint algorithm, which handles inequalities as well as equalities. SwiftUI reuses the priority idea, and size classes extend constraints to iPad split view. Search 'Cassowary constraint solver', 'UIStackView distribution' or 'size classes' next.
